baslik: PersistentVolumeClaim stuck in Pending forever
soru: I created a PVC for my database pod and it's stuck Pending, so the pod is stuck too. `kubectl get pvc` shows Pending, `kubectl describe pvc` mentions 'no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set'. This is a bare-metal cluster I set up with kubeadm. What's missing?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: On a kubeadm bare-metal cluster there is no cloud provider to dynamically provision volumes, and you have no default StorageClass, so a PVC requesting dynamic provisioning waits forever. You need either a provisioner or manually created PVs.

Quickest path for a single-node/dev cluster: install a local-path provisioner (Rancher's `local-path-provisioner` is one YAML apply) and mark it as the default StorageClass. Then your PVC binds automatically using a host directory.

If you want to do it manually, create a PersistentVolume with matching `storageClassName`, capacity and accessModes, and the PVC will bind to it. The class name on PV and PVC must match, including the empty-string case.
Check that your PVC isn't requesting an accessMode the backing storage can't satisfy, e.g. ReadWriteMany on storage that only supports ReadWriteOnce, that also leaves it Pending.
Set the provisioner's class as default with the annotation `storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"` so future PVCs without an explicit class also bind.

baslik: Pods don't pick up new values after I update a ConfigMap
soru: I updated a ConfigMap with new application settings and applied it. But my running pods keep using the old values. I expected them to refresh. Do I have to restart the pods manually every time config changes, or is there a way to make them notice the update?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: It depends on how you consume the ConfigMap. If you inject values as environment variables, they are read once at container start and never update, you must recreate the pods. If you mount the ConfigMap as a volume, the files DO update automatically, but with a delay (kubelet sync period, up to ~1 minute), and your app must re-read the file.

The common pattern to force a rollout on config change is `kubectl rollout restart deployment/myapp`. This recreates pods cleanly with the new config and respects your rolling-update strategy, no downtime if you have replicas.

A neat trick to make changes automatic in CI: put a hash of the ConfigMap content into a pod template annotation. When the config changes the hash changes, the template changes, and Kubernetes does a rollout for you. Helm and Kustomize both support this.

If you mounted as a volume and still don't see updates, check you didn't use `subPath` for the mount, files mounted with subPath are NOT updated when the ConfigMap changes, that's a documented limitation.

cozum: It depends on how you consume the ConfigMap. If you inject values as environment variables, they are read once at container start and never update, you must recreate the pods. If you mount the ConfigMap as a volume, the files DO update automatically, but with a delay (kubelet sync period, up to ~1 minute), and your app must re-read the file.

baslik: One node shows NotReady and pods won't schedule on it
soru: One of my three worker nodes flipped to NotReady and now pods are getting evicted from it and piling up Pending elsewhere. `kubectl get nodes` shows it NotReady. The machine itself is up, I can SSH in. What causes a node to go NotReady and how do I bring it back?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: NotReady means the kubelet on that node stopped reporting healthy heartbeats to the control plane. SSH in and check `systemctl status kubelet` first, a crashed or stopped kubelet is the most common cause. `journalctl -u kubelet -f` will show why.

Very often it's disk pressure or the container runtime. Run `df -h` on the node, a full disk triggers DiskPressure and the kubelet marks itself NotReady and evicts pods. Clearing space and restarting kubelet usually recovers it.
Check the container runtime too: `systemctl status containerd` (or docker). If the runtime is down the kubelet can't manage containers and reports NotReady. Restart containerd then kubelet.

Look at `kubectl describe node <node>` Conditions, it tells you exactly which condition is bad: MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure or a network/CNI problem. If the CNI plugin pod (Calico/Flannel) crashed on that node, networking is gone and the node goes NotReady.
Mine was a full /var/lib/containerd from old images. `crictl rmi --prune` freed space, `systemctl restart kubelet` and the node went Ready within a minute.

cozum: NotReady means the kubelet on that node stopped reporting healthy heartbeats to the control plane. SSH in and check `systemctl status kubelet` first, a crashed or stopped kubelet is the most common cause. `journalctl -u kubelet -f` will show why.
reference_summary: One node shows NotReady and pods won't schedule on it. Resolution: NotReady means the kubelet on that node stopped reporting healthy heartbeats to the control plane.

baslik: ModuleNotFoundError even though I pip installed the package
soru: I ran `pip install requests` and it said successfully installed, but when I run my script `import requests` throws ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'. I'm on a Mac with both Python 2 and Python 3. I've tried reinstalling several times. Why can't Python find a package I just installed?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: This is nearly always a mismatch between the pip that installed and the python that runs your script. You have multiple Pythons, and `pip` may map to a different interpreter than `python`. Check with `which python` and `which pip`, and `pip --version` prints the python it's tied to.

The robust fix is to always install via the interpreter you'll run: `python3 -m pip install requests`. Using `python -m pip` guarantees the package lands in that exact interpreter's site-packages instead of some other Python's.

Best practice is a virtual environment: `python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate && pip install requests`. Inside the venv there's only one python and one pip, and this whole class of confusion disappears.
If you're in VS Code or Jupyter, also check the selected interpreter/kernel, the editor may be running a different Python than your terminal. Bottom-left interpreter picker in VS Code.
Confirm where it landed with `python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"` and `pip show requests` (Location line). When those two paths line up, the import works.

reference_summary: ModuleNotFoundError even though I pip installed the package. Resolution: This is nearly always a mismatch between the pip that installed and the python that runs your script.

baslik: IndentationError: unexpected indent / inconsistent use of tabs and spaces
soru: My Python script throws 'TabError: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation'. The code looks perfectly aligned in my editor. It ran fine yesterday. I copied a function from a tutorial into my file and now the whole thing won't run. How do I find and fix the mixed indentation?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Python 3 forbids mixing tabs and spaces in the same block. Your editor renders them at the same width so it looks aligned, but some lines are tabs and others are spaces. The pasted tutorial code almost certainly used a different convention than your file.
Turn on 'show whitespace' / 'render whitespace' in your editor to see tabs vs spaces directly. In VS Code it's View > Render Whitespace; tabs show as arrows, spaces as dots.

The fix: pick spaces (PEP 8 recommends 4 spaces) and convert. In VS Code, set 'Editor: Insert Spaces' on, then run 'Convert Indentation to Spaces' from the command palette. That normalizes the whole file in one go.
From the command line you can also run `python -m tabnanny yourfile.py` which points to the exact line where indentation becomes inconsistent, very handy for big files.
Going forward, add a .editorconfig with indent_style = space, indent_size = 4 so every contributor's editor agrees and this never recurs.

cozum: Python 3 forbids mixing tabs and spaces in the same block. Your editor renders them at the same width so it looks aligned, but some lines are tabs and others are spaces. The pasted tutorial code almost certainly used a different convention than your file.
reference_summary: IndentationError: unexpected indent / inconsistent use of tabs and spaces. Resolution: Python 3 forbids mixing tabs and spaces in the same block.

baslik: UnicodeDecodeError when reading a text file
soru: I'm reading a CSV exported from Excel with open('data.csv').read() and Python throws UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x... The file opens fine in Excel and Notepad. This only happens with files that have accented characters or the pound/euro symbols. How do I read it correctly?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: The file isn't UTF-8. Python defaults to your locale encoding (often UTF-8), but Excel on Windows frequently saves as cp1252/Windows-1252 or adds a BOM. The byte it choked on is a character that's valid in the file's real encoding but not in UTF-8.
If it's Windows-1252, open with the right encoding explicitly: `open('data.csv', encoding='cp1252')`. For Excel CSVs that's the most common answer and the accented characters come through correctly.
If there's a byte-order mark at the start (you'd see a stray char on the first field), use `encoding='utf-8-sig'`, which strips the BOM that Excel adds when you 'Save as CSV UTF-8'.

When you genuinely don't know the encoding, the `charset-normalizer` or `chardet` library can detect it: `from charset_normalizer import from_path; print(from_path('data.csv').best().encoding)`. Then open with that.

If you just want to not crash and don't mind losing a few odd bytes, `open('data.csv', encoding='utf-8', errors='replace')` will substitute unknown bytes instead of raising, but fixing the encoding properly is better.

cozum: The file isn't UTF-8. Python defaults to your locale encoding (often UTF-8), but Excel on Windows frequently saves as cp1252/Windows-1252 or adds a BOM. The byte it choked on is a character that's valid in the file's real encoding but not in UTF-8.
reference_summary: UnicodeDecodeError when reading a text file. Resolution: The file isn't UTF-8.

baslik: Function with a default list argument remembers values between calls
soru: I have a function `def add(item, target=[]): target.append(item); return target`. The first call works, but on the second call the list already contains the item from the first call. I never passed a list in. It's like the default is shared. Is this a bug in Python?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: It's not a bug, it's the single most famous Python gotcha. Default argument values are evaluated ONCE at function definition time, not on each call. So `target=[]` creates one list that is reused for every call that doesn't supply its own, and your appends accumulate in it.
The idiomatic fix is to default to None and create the list inside: `def add(item, target=None):` then `if target is None: target = []`. Now each call without an argument gets a fresh list.

This applies to any mutable default: lists, dicts, sets, and even things like datetime.now() which would freeze to the import-time value. The None sentinel pattern is the standard solution for all of them.
If you want to detect these in your codebase, pylint (W0102 dangerous-default-value) and ruff both flag mutable default arguments automatically.
Switching to the None default fixed it immediately for me, every call now returns a list with only the items I added in that call.

cozum: It's not a bug, it's the single most famous Python gotcha. Default argument values are evaluated ONCE at function definition time, not on each call. So `target=[]` creates one list that is reused for every call that doesn't supply its own, and your appends accumulate in it.
reference_summary: Function with a default list argument remembers values between calls. Resolution: It's not a bug, it's the single most famous Python gotcha.

baslik: Should I use venv, virtualenv, conda or pipenv? Totally confused
soru: I'm learning Python and every tutorial uses a different tool to manage packages: venv, virtualenv, conda, pipenv, poetry. I just want to keep project dependencies separate so I don't break things globally. Which one should a beginner actually use and why are there so many?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: For a beginner doing general Python, use the built-in `venv`. It ships with Python 3, needs nothing extra, and does exactly what you asked: isolates each project's packages. `python3 -m venv venv` then activate it. Learn this first; the others are variations on the same idea.

Quick map of the landscape: virtualenv is the older third-party version of venv (slightly more features, rarely needed now). conda is for data science and can install non-Python things (C libraries, CUDA) and manage Python itself, great for scientific stacks. pipenv and poetry add lockfiles and dependency resolution on top of venv for apps you'll share.

Rule of thumb: plain `venv` + `pip` + a requirements.txt covers 90% of learning and small projects. Move to poetry when you're publishing a package or need reproducible locked builds. Use conda specifically if you're doing numpy/scipy/ML and hitting compiled-dependency pain.
Whatever you pick, the golden rule is: never `pip install` into the system Python. Always have an activated environment. That alone prevents the 'I broke my OS Python' disasters.
I went venv for everything as a beginner and only adopted poetry a year later when I started publishing libraries. No regrets, venv is plenty.

cozum: For a beginner doing general Python, use the built-in `venv`. It ships with Python 3, needs nothing extra, and does exactly what you asked: isolates each project's packages. `python3 -m venv venv` then activate it. Learn this first; the others are variations on the same idea.
reference_summary: Should I use venv, virtualenv, conda or pipenv? Totally confused. Resolution: For a beginner doing general Python, use the built-in `venv`.

baslik: requests raises SSLError / CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED behind a corporate proxy
soru: Using the requests library, every HTTPS call fails with SSLError: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED. This is on my work laptop behind a corporate proxy. The same URLs open fine in Chrome. I know I can pass verify=False but people say that's dangerous. What's the right way to fix this properly?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Your company does TLS interception: the proxy presents its own root CA, which Chrome trusts (it's in the OS/enterprise store) but Python's requests uses its own bundled CA store via certifi, which doesn't include the corporate root. Hence the verification failure.

The correct fix is to give Python the corporate CA. Export the company root certificate (your IT can provide the .pem, or grab it from Chrome's certificate viewer) and point requests at it: `requests.get(url, verify='/path/corp-ca.pem')`, or set the env var `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/corp-ca.pem` so it applies everywhere.

To make it permanent for all tools, append the corporate root to certifi's bundle: `python -c "import certifi; print(certifi.where())"` gives the path, then add the PEM there (or better, use the `pip-system-certs` package which makes requests trust the OS store automatically).

Avoid `verify=False`. It silences the warning but disables certificate validation entirely, meaning anyone on the network could MITM you. It's fine for a throwaway local test, never for anything real.
Setting REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE to our exported corp CA fixed every script at once without touching code. IT had the .pem on the intranet.

baslik: Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000
soru: My Express app won't start, it throws 'Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000'. This happens a lot during development when I stop and restart with nodemon. Sometimes restarting my whole machine fixes it but that's silly. How do I find and kill whatever is holding port 3000, and how do I stop this happening?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: A previous node process is still bound to 3000, usually an orphan left when nodemon restarted or a crash didn't release the port. Find it: on macOS/Linux `lsof -i :3000` gives the PID, then `kill -9 <PID>`. On Windows `netstat -ano | findstr :3000` then `taskkill /PID <pid> /F`.
A one-liner to free it on Unix: `kill -9 $(lsof -t -i:3000)`. Or install `npx kill-port 3000` which works cross-platform.

To prevent it, handle shutdown signals so the server closes the socket cleanly: listen for SIGINT/SIGTERM and call `server.close()`. Orphaned ports usually come from the process being killed before it released the listener.
If it happens specifically with nodemon, you sometimes get a double-start. Make sure you don't also have the app running in another terminal or a VS Code launch config bound to the same port.
For dev resilience, read the port from an env var and fall back, or use a tiny helper that retries on the next free port. But the real fix is clean shutdown handling so the orphan never lingers.

cozum: A previous node process is still bound to 3000, usually an orphan left when nodemon restarted or a crash didn't release the port. Find it: on macOS/Linux `lsof -i :3000` gives the PID, then `kill -9 <PID>`. On Windows `netstat -ano | findstr :3000` then `taskkill /PID <pid> /F`.
reference_summary: Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000. Resolution: A previous node process is still bound to 3000, usually an orphan left when nodemon restarted or a crash didn't release the port.

baslik: Error: Cannot find module after deploying, works locally
soru: My Node app runs perfectly on my Mac but on the Linux server it crashes with 'Error: Cannot find module ./Routes/User'. The file is definitely there, I can see Routes/user.js. I copied the project over with git. Why would it find the module locally but not on the server?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Case sensitivity. macOS's default filesystem is case-INsensitive, Linux is case-SENSITIVE. Your require says `./Routes/User` but the file is `routes/user.js`. On your Mac that matches anyway; on Linux it's a different name and fails. This bites almost everyone deploying Mac to Linux.
Fix the require to match the real filename exactly, including folder casing: `require('./routes/user')`. Then make all your imports consistent with the actual file/folder names.

To catch these before deploy, you can enable `forceConsistentCasingInFileNames` if you use TypeScript, or add an ESLint rule. They'll flag the mismatch on your Mac where it would otherwise pass silently.

Also double check it's not a missing dependency: if `node_modules` wasn't installed on the server (you shouldn't commit it), run `npm ci` there. But your specific path with a capital folder is the classic case-sensitivity bug.
Renaming the import to the exact lowercase path fixed it instantly on the server. I now keep all folders lowercase to avoid the whole problem.

cozum: Case sensitivity. macOS's default filesystem is case-INsensitive, Linux is case-SENSITIVE. Your require says `./Routes/User` but the file is `routes/user.js`. On your Mac that matches anyway; on Linux it's a different name and fails. This bites almost everyone deploying Mac to Linux.
reference_summary: Error: Cannot find module after deploying, works locally. Resolution: Case sensitivity.

baslik: My async function returns undefined / Promise instead of the value
soru: I have an async function that fetches data and returns it, but when I call it the caller gets a pending Promise or undefined instead of the actual data. console.log inside the function shows the right value. I'm clearly misunderstanding async/await. What's going on?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: An async function ALWAYS returns a Promise, never the bare value. When you call it you get a Promise that will later resolve to your value. To get the value you must `await` the call (inside another async function) or use `.then()`.

So `const data = getData()` gives you a Promise. You want `const data = await getData()`. The log inside works because there you're looking at the resolved value directly; the caller is looking at the wrapper.

If you're getting `undefined` specifically, you probably forgot to `return` inside the async function, or you returned before an inner await finished. Make sure every promise in the chain is awaited and the final value is returned.
You can only use `await` inside an async function (or at top level in ESM modules). If the caller can't be async, use `getData().then(data => { ... })` instead.
Adding await at the call site fixed it. The trap is that forgetting await doesn't error, it just silently hands you a Promise, so the bug is easy to miss.

cozum: An async function ALWAYS returns a Promise, never the bare value. When you call it you get a Promise that will later resolve to your value. To get the value you must `await` the call (inside another async function) or use `.then()`.
reference_summary: My async function returns undefined / Promise instead of the value. Resolution: An async function ALWAYS returns a Promise, never the bare value.

baslik: CORS error: blocked by CORS policy, No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin'
soru: My React frontend on localhost:3000 calls my Express API on localhost:5000 and the browser blocks it: 'has been blocked by CORS policy: No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header'. The API works fine when I hit it with curl or Postman. Why does the browser block it and how do I allow my frontend?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: CORS is a browser security feature, that's why curl and Postman work (they don't enforce it) but the browser blocks the cross-origin request. localhost:3000 and localhost:5000 are different origins (different port), so the browser requires your API to opt in with the right headers.

Easiest fix in Express: `npm i cors` then `app.use(cors())` to allow all origins during development, or scope it: `app.use(cors({ origin: 'http://localhost:3000', credentials: true }))` for production safety.

If you send cookies/auth, you must set `credentials: true` on the server AND `withCredentials: true` (or fetch credentials: 'include') on the client, and the server's allowed origin cannot be the wildcard `*` in that case, it must be the explicit origin.

For preflighted requests (custom headers, PUT/DELETE), the browser sends an OPTIONS request first; the cors middleware handles that automatically, but if you hand-roll headers make sure you respond to OPTIONS.
A cleaner long-term setup is to proxy API calls through your frontend dev server (CRA's `proxy` field or Vite's server.proxy) so everything is same-origin in dev and CORS doesn't apply at all.

cozum: CORS is a browser security feature, that's why curl and Postman work (they don't enforce it) but the browser blocks the cross-origin request. localhost:3000 and localhost:5000 are different origins (different port), so the browser requires your API to opt in with the right headers.

baslik: Node process memory keeps climbing until it crashes (heap out of memory)
soru: My long-running Node service slowly grows in memory over hours and eventually dies with 'JavaScript heap out of memory'. Restarting fixes it temporarily. It handles a lot of requests. How do I find what's leaking without just throwing more RAM at it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: First confirm it's a real leak vs normal growth: take heap snapshots over time. Start the process with `node --inspect`, open chrome://inspect, and capture a heap snapshot early and again after load. Compare them, the 'Comparison' view shows which object types grew, that's your leak.

The usual suspects in Node: event listeners added in a hot path without removal (you'll see a MaxListenersExceededWarning), unbounded caches/Maps that never evict, closures capturing large objects, and global arrays you push to but never clear.

A fast tactical check: log `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` periodically. If it climbs monotonically and never drops after GC, it's a leak. You can also run with `--expose-gc` and force GC to confirm the memory isn't reclaimable.
Common real cause: registering `.on('event', ...)` per request instead of once. Every request adds a listener that's never removed. Move listener registration out of the request handler.
For us it was a module-level Map used as a cache that grew forever. Switching to an LRU cache with a max size (e.g. the `lru-cache` package) flattened the memory curve completely.

cozum: First confirm it's a real leak vs normal growth: take heap snapshots over time. Start the process with `node --inspect`, open chrome://inspect, and capture a heap snapshot early and again after load. Compare them, the 'Comparison' view shows which object types grew, that's your leak.

baslik: npm audit reports 47 vulnerabilities, npm audit fix doesn't clear them
soru: Every time I run npm install I get a scary report of dozens of vulnerabilities, several 'critical'. `npm audit fix` clears a few but most remain and it says they require breaking changes. I'm not sure which actually matter or whether `npm audit fix --force` is safe. How should I handle this?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: First, don't panic at the raw count. The vast majority of npm audit findings are in transitive devDependencies (build tools, test runners) that never run in production, and many are low-severity ReDoS issues that don't apply to your usage. The number is almost always inflated relative to real risk.
Triage by where the dep lives and whether it ships. `npm audit --omit=dev` shows only production dependencies, that's the set that actually matters for a deployed service. Focus your effort there.

Avoid `npm audit fix --force` casually, it installs major version bumps that can and will break your app. Read what it wants to upgrade; if it's a major version of something central, do that deliberately and test.
For transitive deps you can't directly control, use the `overrides` field in package.json to pin a fixed version of the nested package without waiting for the parent to update.

Realistically: run `npm audit --omit=dev`, fix the production criticals/highs deliberately, and accept that dev-only advisories with no exploit path can wait. Chasing zero on the full report is usually a waste of time.

The vast majority of npm audit findings are in transitive devDependencies (build tools, test runners) that never run in production, and many are low-severity ReDoS issues that don't apply to your usage. The number is almost always inflated relative to real risk.

baslik: FATAL: sorry, too many clients already
soru: My web app intermittently fails with 'FATAL: sorry, too many clients already' from Postgres, especially under load. max_connections is 100. The app is a Node API with several instances. Should I just raise max_connections, or is that a band-aid? What's the right fix?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Raising max_connections is usually the wrong first move. Each Postgres connection is a separate backend process costing real memory (work_mem etc.), so going to 500 can exhaust RAM and slow everything down. The real issue is almost always that your app opens too many connections or leaks them.

Use a connection pool and bound it. In Node with `pg`, create ONE `Pool` per process with a sensible `max` (e.g. 10) and reuse it, never `new Client()` per request. If you run 8 app instances times 10 = 80 connections, comfortably under 100.

For serverless or many instances, put PgBouncer in front in transaction-pooling mode. Hundreds of app connections multiplex onto a small number of real Postgres connections. This is the standard fix at scale.

Check for leaks: `SELECT count(*), state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state`. Lots of 'idle in transaction' means your code opens a transaction and forgets to commit/rollback, holding connections hostage. Fix that and connection use drops sharply.
We capped the pool at 10 per instance and added PgBouncer; the 'too many clients' errors vanished and we never touched max_connections.

cozum: Raising max_connections is usually the wrong first move. Each Postgres connection is a separate backend process costing real memory (work_mem etc.), so going to 500 can exhaust RAM and slow everything down. The real issue is almost always that your app opens too many connections or leaks them.

baslik: A query that was fast is now very slow on a big table
soru: I have a query filtering a 20-million-row table by a status column and a date range. It used to be quick, now it takes 30+ seconds. I have an index on status. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a Seq Scan. Why is it ignoring my index and how do I speed it up?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and look at what it's actually doing. A Seq Scan despite an index usually means one of: the index isn't selective enough (status has few distinct values so the planner thinks scanning is cheaper), stale statistics, or the index doesn't cover the date filter.

If you filter by status AND date, a single-column index on status alone often loses to a seq scan. Create a composite index matching your WHERE: `CREATE INDEX ON t (status, created_at)`. Order matters, put the equality column first, the range column second.

Stale stats make the planner misjudge row counts. Run `ANALYZE t;` (or check autovacuum is keeping up). After a big data change the planner may be using ancient estimates and choosing a seq scan wrongly.
If status has very few values and you mostly query one rare value, a partial index is ideal: `CREATE INDEX ON t (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'`. Tiny index, very fast for that hot path.
Composite (status, created_at) plus an ANALYZE took ours from 30s to ~40ms. Always confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the new index is actually used (Index Scan, not Seq Scan).

baslik: Connections stuck in 'idle in transaction' blocking other queries
soru: Some of my updates hang and time out. Looking at pg_stat_activity I see several connections in state 'idle in transaction' that have been there for a long time, and they seem to hold locks that block my writes. What does this state mean and how do I prevent it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: 'idle in transaction' means a client ran BEGIN (or a statement that opened a transaction) and then went idle without COMMIT or ROLLBACK. The transaction is still open, so it keeps any locks it took and prevents vacuum from cleaning rows, which is why your writes block.

It's an application bug: code opens a transaction, then does something slow (an HTTP call, waits for user input, or just forgets to commit), or your ORM didn't close the session. Find the offenders with `SELECT pid, state, xact_start, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='idle in transaction' ORDER BY xact_start`.

Immediate relief: terminate the stuck ones with `SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)`. But that's a band-aid; fix the code so transactions are short and always committed/rolled back, ideally with a `try/finally` or your ORM's context manager.
Add a safety net on the server: set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` (e.g. '30s'). Postgres will automatically abort transactions left idle too long, so a buggy client can't hold locks forever.
Setting idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 30s plus fixing one route that opened a transaction before an external API call eliminated the blocking for us.

cozum: 'idle in transaction' means a client ran BEGIN (or a statement that opened a transaction) and then went idle without COMMIT or ROLLBACK. The transaction is still open, so it keeps any locks it took and prevents vacuum from cleaning rows, which is why your writes block.
reference_summary: Connections stuck in 'idle in transaction' blocking other queries. Resolution: 'idle in transaction' means a client ran BEGIN (or a statement that opened a transaction) and then went idle without COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

baslik: permission denied for schema public on a new database (PG 15)
soru: After upgrading to Postgres 15 I created a new user and database, but when that user tries to CREATE TABLE it gets 'permission denied for schema public'. This worked fine on Postgres 13. The user owns the database. What changed and how do I grant the right access?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Postgres 15 tightened a long-standing security wart: the public schema is no longer writable by everyone by default. Previously all users could create objects in public; now they can't unless explicitly granted. That's why your PG13 habit broke.

Grant the privilege explicitly. Connected as a superuser or the database owner, run `GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA public TO myuser;` (or at least `GRANT USAGE, CREATE ON SCHEMA public TO myuser;`). Then the user can create tables again.

Better practice on 15+: give each app its own schema and make it the owner. `CREATE SCHEMA app AUTHORIZATION myuser;` then set the user's `search_path` to that schema. Cleaner isolation than everyone sharing public.
Note that owning the database is not the same as owning the public schema, that's the subtle part. The schema's default owner is the bootstrap superuser, so you grant on the schema specifically.
GRANT CREATE ON SCHEMA public TO myuser fixed it immediately. The PG15 release notes flag this as an intentional, security-motivated change.

cozum: Postgres 15 tightened a long-standing security wart: the public schema is no longer writable by everyone by default. Previously all users could create objects in public; now they can't unless explicitly granted. That's why your PG13 habit broke.
reference_summary: permission denied for schema public on a new database (PG 15). Resolution: Postgres 15 tightened a long-standing security wart: the public schema is no longer writable by everyone by default.

baslik: duplicate key value violates unique constraint on an id column after a data import
soru: After importing data with explicit id values into a table that uses a SERIAL/identity primary key, new inserts now fail with 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint (pkey)'. It's trying to insert id=5 when 5 already exists. The import included ids. How do I get the auto-increment back in sync?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: When you insert rows with explicit id values, Postgres does NOT advance the underlying sequence. So the sequence still thinks the next id is 5 even though you imported ids up to 5000. The next auto-insert collides. This is expected behaviour after a manual id import.

Reset the sequence to past the max existing id: `SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('mytable','id'), (SELECT MAX(id) FROM mytable));`. Using pg_get_serial_sequence avoids guessing the sequence name. New inserts will then start above the imported max.

If the table is empty when you reset, use the third argument: `setval(seq, value, false)` so the next value is exactly `value` rather than value+1. For a populated table the two-arg form (defaults is_called=true) is what you want.
Going forward, either don't import the id column (let the DB assign), or if you must keep ids, run the setval as the last step of your import script every time.
The setval-with-MAX(id) one-liner fixed it instantly and inserts resumed without collisions.

cozum: When you insert rows with explicit id values, Postgres does NOT advance the underlying sequence. So the sequence still thinks the next id is 5 even though you imported ids up to 5000. The next auto-insert collides. This is expected behaviour after a manual id import.
reference_summary: duplicate key value violates unique constraint on an id column after a data import. Resolution: When you insert rows with explicit id values, Postgres does NOT advance the underlying sequence.

baslik: pg_dump vs continuous backups, what should a small team actually do?
soru: We run a single Postgres instance for a small SaaS. Right now 'backups' are a nightly pg_dump to a file. I'm worried that's not enough, if the server dies at 5pm we lose a day of data. What's a realistic backup strategy that isn't enterprise-level overkill?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Your nightly pg_dump is a fine logical backup baseline but you're right about the gap: it only protects you to the last dump, so worst case you lose ~24h. For a SaaS that's usually unacceptable. You want point-in-time recovery (PITR) on top.

The standard approach: take periodic base backups (pg_basebackup) and continuously archive WAL files (archive_command shipping to S3 or another host). With WAL archiving you can restore to any moment, so a 5pm crash loses seconds, not a day.

If you'd rather not operate PITR yourself, the pragmatic answer for a small team is a managed Postgres (RDS, Cloud SQL, Supabase) which gives you automated PITR and retained snapshots out of the box. Often cheaper than your time.

Keep the nightly pg_dump too, it's your logical, version-portable backup and protects against logical corruption or 'someone dropped a table' that a physical restore to 4:59pm would also undo. Different failure modes.
Crucially: test restores regularly. An untested backup isn't a backup. We restore last night's dump into a scratch instance weekly in CI to prove it works.

baslik: Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost' (using password: YES)
soru: I can't log into MySQL as root anymore: 'Access denied for user root@localhost (using password: YES)'. I'm sure the password is right. This is on a fresh Ubuntu install. I never explicitly set a root password. How do I get in and reset it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: On modern Ubuntu MySQL/MariaDB, root@localhost authenticates with the `auth_socket` plugin by default, not a password. That means root can only log in as the OS root user, with no password: `sudo mysql` works, while `mysql -u root -p` is denied no matter what you type.

So first try `sudo mysql`. You'll get in. If you want a real password login, switch the plugin: `ALTER USER 'root'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED WITH mysql_native_password BY 'yourpassword';` then FLUSH PRIVILEGES.

If you genuinely lost the password and socket auth isn't set, restart mysqld with `--skip-grant-tables`, connect, FLUSH PRIVILEGES, then ALTER USER to set a new password, then restart normally. Do this with the network port closed for safety.

Best practice is to leave root on auth_socket (it's more secure, no password to leak) and create a separate application user with a password and only the privileges it needs, rather than using root from your app.
`sudo mysql` got me straight in, the password was never the issue, it was the auth_socket plugin. I created a dedicated app user after that.

baslik: Incorrect string value when inserting emoji / certain characters
soru: Inserting user text that contains an emoji fails with 'Incorrect string value: \xF0\x9F...'. Plain text saves fine. The column is utf8. I thought utf8 supported everything. Why does an emoji break it and how do I fix it without losing data?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: MySQL's `utf8` is a historical lie, it's actually `utf8mb3` and only stores up to 3 bytes per character, which excludes emoji and many CJK and supplementary characters (those need 4 bytes). The emoji is a 4-byte character, hence the error.

The fix is to use the real UTF-8, called `utf8mb4`. Convert the column/table: `ALTER TABLE t CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;`. Also set the database default and the connection charset to utf8mb4.

Don't forget the connection itself: the client connection charset must also be utf8mb4 or the 4-byte char gets mangled in transit. In your driver set charset=utf8mb4 (e.g. in the DSN / connection options).
Check my.cnf has `character-set-server = utf8mb4` and `collation-server = utf8mb4_unicode_ci` so new tables default correctly and you don't have to remember each time.
Converting the table to utf8mb4 and setting the connection charset to utf8mb4 fixed emoji inserts with no data loss. utf8mb4 is a strict superset of utf8mb3 so existing data is unaffected.

baslik: Lost connection to MySQL server during query on large imports
soru: When importing a big SQL dump or running a bulk insert, I get 'Lost connection to MySQL server during query' partway through. Small queries are fine. The server has plenty of RAM. What setting is cutting me off and how do I import big data reliably?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: The usual culprit is `max_allowed_packet`. A single large statement (a fat multi-row INSERT or a big BLOB) exceeds the packet size limit and the server drops the connection. Raise it on BOTH server and client, e.g. `max_allowed_packet=256M`.
Set it in my.cnf under [mysqld] and restart, or for a one-off import pass it to the client: `mysql --max_allowed_packet=256M dbname < dump.sql`. The client limit matters too, not just the server.
Two other timeouts can cause it on long imports: `net_read_timeout` and `wait_timeout`. If a single statement runs longer than these the server hangs up. Raise them for the import session.

For very large dumps, importing as many smaller statements helps, mysqldump's default extended-insert batching is usually fine, but if someone produced one giant INSERT, splitting it avoids the packet limit entirely.
Bumping max_allowed_packet to 256M on the client side of the import was the fix for me, the dump had some huge rows.

reference_summary: Lost connection to MySQL server during query on large imports. Resolution: The usual culprit is `max_allowed_packet`.

baslik: Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
soru: Under concurrent load, some transactions fail with 'Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction' (InnoDB). It's intermittent. The transactions update a couple of related tables. Is this a bug, and how do I make it stop?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Deadlocks aren't bugs per se, they happen when two transactions lock the same rows in opposite order and each waits for the other. InnoDB detects this and kills one (the victim) so the other proceeds. The error is InnoDB telling you it broke the cycle.

Two-pronged fix. Prevention: always acquire locks in a consistent order across your code (e.g. always update table A before B, and update rows in ascending id order). Most deadlocks come from inconsistent ordering between code paths.

Equally important: expect and handle them. Wrap the transaction in retry logic, on deadlock (error 1213) wait a few ms and retry the whole transaction a couple of times. Even with good ordering, occasional deadlocks under load are normal and retrying is the correct response.

Diagnose the specific case with `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` right after a deadlock, the LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section shows exactly which two statements and locks collided. That usually reveals the ordering problem.
We standardized update order and added a 3-try retry wrapper, deadlocks dropped to near zero and the rare survivor is handled transparently.

baslik: ERROR 1055: not in GROUP BY clause and contains nonaggregated column (only_full_group_by)
soru: A GROUP BY query that worked on our old MySQL 5.6 server now errors on 5.7/8.0 with 'this is incompatible with sql_mode=only_full_group_by'. The query selects several columns but only groups by one. What changed and what's the correct fix, I don't want to just disable the mode blindly?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: MySQL 5.7+ enables ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY by default, which enforces the SQL standard: every selected non-aggregated column must appear in GROUP BY (or be functionally dependent on it). Older MySQL silently returned arbitrary values for the extra columns, which was a footgun, now it errors.

The right fix depends on intent. If those extra columns are genuinely one-per-group, add them to GROUP BY. If you want a representative value, wrap them in an aggregate like `ANY_VALUE(col)`, `MAX(col)`, or `MIN(col)` to make your intent explicit.

Often the query was subtly wrong all along, returning a random row's value for the ungrouped columns. The error is a chance to express what you actually meant, e.g. the latest row per group via a window function or a join to a grouped subquery.

Disabling the mode (`sql_mode` without ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY) makes it run like 5.6 again, but you keep the indeterminate-results risk. Acceptable as a temporary migration step, not a good permanent state.
We rewrote the handful of offending queries with ANY_VALUE where the column truly was constant per group, and a proper window function where it wasn't. Left the safe mode on.

baslik: Nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway in front of my app
soru: Nginx is reverse-proxying to my app (a gunicorn/Node backend) and randomly returns 502 Bad Gateway. The app itself seems up, I can curl it directly on its port. The Nginx error log mentions 'connect() failed' or 'upstream prematurely closed connection'. How do I track down and fix the 502?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: 502 means Nginx couldn't get a valid response from the upstream. Read /var/log/nginx/error.log, the exact phrasing tells you which case it is: 'connect() failed (111: Connection refused)' = upstream not listening where Nginx expects; 'upstream prematurely closed connection' = the app crashed/closed mid-response; 'upstream timed out' = app too slow.

If it's 'connection refused', your proxy_pass target is wrong, check the host:port and that the app binds that interface. If you proxy to 127.0.0.1:8000 but the app binds a unix socket or a different port, you get refused 502s.

'Upstream prematurely closed' usually means the backend worker died (out of memory, an unhandled exception, or a worker timeout). Check the app's own logs at the same timestamps; the fix is on the app side (raise worker timeout, fix the crash).
'Upstream timed out' is fixed by aligning timeouts: raise `proxy_read_timeout`/`proxy_connect_timeout` in Nginx AND the worker timeout in gunicorn so a slow-but-valid response isn't cut off.
Mine was gunicorn workers being killed by the default 30s timeout on a slow endpoint; raising gunicorn --timeout and nginx proxy_read_timeout to 120s ended the 502s.

cozum: 502 means Nginx couldn't get a valid response from the upstream. Read /var/log/nginx/error.log, the exact phrasing tells you which case it is: 'connect() failed (111: Connection refused)' = upstream not listening where Nginx expects; 'upstream prematurely closed connection' = the app crashed/closed mid-response; 'upstream timed out' = app too slow.

baslik: 413 Request Entity Too Large when uploading files
soru: File uploads above ~1MB fail with '413 Request Entity Too Large' before they even reach my app. Smaller files upload fine. The app's own limit is much higher. This points at Nginx. Which setting limits the upload size and where do I put it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Nginx caps request bodies at 1MB by default via `client_max_body_size`, and rejects anything larger with 413 before it ever reaches your app, which is why your app's higher limit is irrelevant. You need to raise it in Nginx.

Add `client_max_body_size 50M;` (or whatever you need). You can put it in the http, server, or location block, location-level lets you allow big uploads only on the upload endpoint while keeping other routes tight. Reload with `nginx -s reload`.

Don't forget to also raise the limit in your application/framework (e.g. PHP's upload_max_filesize and post_max_size, or your body parser's limit). Both layers must allow the size or you'll hit 413 at one of them.

If you proxy to an upstream, that's fine, client_max_body_size is enforced by the front Nginx; just set it there. For very large uploads also consider `proxy_request_buffering off` so Nginx streams instead of buffering the whole body to disk.
Setting client_max_body_size 50M in the location block and reloading fixed the uploads instantly.

baslik: SPA routes give 404 on refresh but work when navigating in-app
soru: My single-page app (React) works when I click around, but refreshing on a deep route like /dashboard/settings gives an Nginx 404. The index loads fine at /. I understand the server doesn't have those files. How do I configure Nginx so all routes fall back to index.html?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Right, the routes only exist client-side; on refresh the browser asks Nginx for /dashboard/settings as a real file, which doesn't exist, so 404. You need a fallback that serves index.html for any path the filesystem can't satisfy, letting the SPA router take over.

The standard recipe is `try_files`: in your location block use `location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; }`. Nginx tries the exact file, then a directory, then falls back to index.html for everything else.
Keep real assets working: put a more specific location for static files with caching so a missing asset still 404s honestly instead of returning HTML, which causes confusing MIME errors.
Make sure `root` points at your build output directory (the folder containing index.html and the static assets), and reload Nginx after editing.
Adding `try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;` fixed deep-link refreshes immediately. Every route now boots the app and the client router renders the right view.

cozum: Right, the routes only exist client-side; on refresh the browser asks Nginx for /dashboard/settings as a real file, which doesn't exist, so 404. You need a fallback that serves index.html for any path the filesystem can't satisfy, letting the SPA router take over.

baslik: Too many redirects after setting up HTTPS behind a load balancer / Cloudflare
soru: I set up an HTTP to HTTPS redirect in Nginx, but now the browser says 'ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS'. The site is behind Cloudflare (or an AWS load balancer). Without Cloudflare it worked. Why does the redirect loop and how do I fix it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Classic redirect loop with a proxy in front. Cloudflare/the LB terminates TLS and talks to your Nginx over plain HTTP. Your Nginx sees HTTP, redirects to HTTPS, Cloudflare forwards that as HTTP again, Nginx redirects again, forever.

The fix is to make Nginx trust the proxy's protocol header instead of the raw connection. Redirect based on `$http_x_forwarded_proto`: `if ($http_x_forwarded_proto != "https") { return 301 https://$host$request_uri; }`. Now Nginx only redirects when the ORIGINAL client request wasn't HTTPS.

Also set Cloudflare's SSL mode to 'Full' (not 'Flexible'). 'Flexible' forces Cloudflare-to-origin to be HTTP regardless, which is exactly what creates the loop. 'Full' or 'Full (strict)' lets the origin be HTTPS and behaves correctly.
If you use a real cert on the origin, 'Full (strict)' is best. If the origin only does HTTP, drop the Nginx redirect entirely and let Cloudflare handle the HTTP to HTTPS upgrade at the edge.
Switching to X-Forwarded-Proto-based redirect and setting Cloudflare to Full stopped the loop.

cozum: Classic redirect loop with a proxy in front. Cloudflare/the LB terminates TLS and talks to your Nginx over plain HTTP. Your Nginx sees HTTP, redirects to HTTPS, Cloudflare forwards that as HTTP again, Nginx redirects again, forever.
reference_summary: Too many redirects after setting up HTTPS behind a load balancer / Cloudflare. Resolution: Classic redirect loop with a proxy in front.

baslik: How do I safely test and reload Nginx config without taking the site down?
soru: I'm scared to touch the Nginx config on a live server because a typo could 502 the whole site. What's the safe workflow to edit, validate, and apply config changes with the least risk of an outage?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Always validate before applying: `nginx -t` parses the config and reports syntax errors and bad directives WITHOUT touching the running server. If it says 'syntax is ok / test is successful', you're safe to reload; if not, fix it first and the live site keeps running untouched.

Apply with a graceful reload, not a restart: `nginx -s reload` (or `systemctl reload nginx`). Reload re-reads config and spins up new worker processes while old ones finish in-flight requests, so there's no dropped connection. `restart` briefly stops the service, avoid it for config changes.

Belt-and-braces workflow: keep the config in version control, edit, run `nginx -t`, reload, and verify with curl. If something's wrong, `git checkout` the previous version and reload back. Recovery is seconds.
On critical systems, test the exact config on a staging box first, or use `nginx -t -c /path/to/new.conf` to test an alternate file before swapping it in.
The habit of `nginx -t && nginx -s reload` (only reload if the test passes) means a typo can never take the site down, the reload simply won't happen.

cozum: Always validate before applying: `nginx -t` parses the config and reports syntax errors and bad directives WITHOUT touching the running server. If it says 'syntax is ok / test is successful', you're safe to reload; if not, fix it first and the live site keeps running untouched.

baslik: Battery draining fast after the latest Android update
soru: After the most recent system update my phone's battery life dropped dramatically, it barely lasts half a day now when it used to last all day. Nothing else changed, same apps, same usage. Is this a known thing after updates and what can I actually do to get my battery life back?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: This is extremely common right after a major update. The system rebuilds app caches and re-indexes media in the background for a day or two, plus apps re-optimize their code, all of which hammers the battery temporarily. Give it 2-3 full charge cycles before judging, it often settles by itself.

If it doesn't settle, go to Settings > Battery > Battery usage and see which app is at the top. A misbehaving app that didn't update cleanly is often the cause. Update all apps from the Play Store, force-stop or reinstall the worst offender.

Check for a stuck wakelock keeping the phone awake. Settings > Battery often shows 'screen on' vs background drain; if background is huge, an app (or a synced account) is preventing deep sleep. Disabling and re-adding the account sometimes clears it.

Wiping the cache partition from recovery (without wiping data) resolves a lot of post-update drain. On many phones: power off, hold Power+Volume Up, choose 'Wipe cache partition'. Your data is untouched.
After my update, drain was caused by Google Play Services re-syncing. It normalized after about two days and clearing the cache partition sped it up. Battery is back to normal now.

cozum: This is extremely common right after a major update. The system rebuilds app caches and re-indexes media in the background for a day or two, plus apps re-optimize their code, all of which hammers the battery temporarily. Give it 2-3 full charge cycles before judging, it often settles by itself.

baslik: Phone connects to WiFi but says 'Connected, no internet'
soru: My Android phone connects to my home WiFi, shows the WiFi icon, but nothing loads, it says 'Connected, no internet'. Other devices on the same network work fine, so it's not the router. Mobile data works on the phone. How do I fix the phone so WiFi actually gets online?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Since other devices work, it's the phone's network state for that SSID. First try the simple reset: forget the network (long-press the WiFi name > Forget), then reconnect and re-enter the password. This clears a bad lease or stale config more often than people expect.

A common cause is a misconfigured private DNS or a stuck DNS setting. Settings > Network > Private DNS, set it to 'Off' or 'Automatic', or try setting DNS to 8.8.8.8. A failing private DNS gives exactly the 'no internet' state with a connected icon.

Toggle Airplane mode on for 10 seconds then off, and reboot the phone. If your phone has a 'WiFi assistant'/'adaptive connectivity' feature that switches to mobile data when WiFi seems weak, disable it, it can wrongly mark a good WiFi as no-internet.

If nothing works, Settings > System > Reset > Reset WiFi, mobile & Bluetooth. This wipes all saved networks and network settings (you'll re-enter WiFi passwords) and clears whatever corrupted state was stuck.
Forgetting the network and turning Private DNS to Automatic fixed it for me, the private DNS host I'd set earlier had gone down and was silently blocking all lookups.

baslik: Storage full but I can't find what's using the space
soru: My phone says storage is full and won't let me take photos or update apps. But when I add up my photos and apps it's nowhere near the total. Settings shows a huge 'Other' or 'System' category. Where is the space actually going and how do I safely reclaim it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: The mysterious bulk is usually app cache and downloaded media inside apps, not the OS. WhatsApp/Telegram media, Spotify/Netflix offline downloads, and browser cache can quietly consume many gigabytes that don't show up as 'photos'. Go into each big app's storage and clear cache/downloads.

Settings > Storage > and tap each category. 'Other'/'System' looking huge is often misattributed cache. Use the built-in 'Free up space' / Files by Google, which finds large files, duplicates, and junk and lets you delete safely.

Messaging apps are the usual giant. In WhatsApp: Settings > Storage and data > Manage storage shows the biggest space hogs (forwarded videos, large media) and lets you bulk-delete them. This alone often frees several GB.
Photos already backed up to Google Photos can be removed from the device: open Photos > Free up space, it deletes only the local copies that are safely in the cloud.
Clearing WhatsApp media and using Files by Google to remove cached junk freed about 9GB for me, the 'Other' category shrank dramatically once the app caches were cleared.

baslik: 'App not installed' error when installing an APK
soru: I'm trying to sideload an APK and I keep getting 'App not installed' with no further detail. The download completes fine. I've enabled 'install from unknown sources'. The same APK installed fine on a friend's phone. What causes this generic failure and how do I get it to install?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: The most common cause is a signature conflict: a version of the same app (same package name) is already installed, possibly from a different source, and the signatures don't match. Uninstall the existing copy completely first, then install the APK. Even a leftover from another user profile counts.

Second common cause: architecture or Android-version mismatch. The APK may be built for arm64 only while your device is different, or it targets a newer minSdk than your Android version. A 'universal' APK or one matching your device's ABI installs cleanly.

A corrupted/partial download also gives this. Re-download the APK and verify the file size matches the source. If it's a split APK (multiple files), a plain installer can't handle it, you need an APKMirror-style installer or to install the bundle.
Not enough free storage triggers it too, despite the unhelpful message. Free up a bit of space and retry.
For me an old version under a second user profile was holding the package name. Removing it from all profiles then reinstalling worked.

baslik: Notifications arrive late or only when I open the app
soru: Some apps (messaging, email) only show notifications when I manually open them, or they arrive hours late. Other apps are fine. This started after I got a new phone. I've checked notifications are enabled for the app. What's stopping timely notifications?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: This is almost always aggressive battery optimization killing the app's background connection. Manufacturer skins (Xiaomi/MIUI, Samsung, OnePlus, Huawei) are the worst offenders. Go to Settings > Battery > and set the affected apps to 'Unrestricted' / exclude them from optimization. That single change fixes most delayed-notification cases.

Also disable 'Adaptive Battery' or 'Deep sleeping apps' for those apps specifically. These features put rarely-used apps to sleep, severing the push connection until you open them, which is exactly your symptom.

Check the app isn't being 'put to sleep' automatically: Settings > Apps > [app] > Battery > Allow background activity / Remove from sleeping apps list. On Samsung there's a separate 'Sleeping apps' and 'Deep sleeping apps' list to clear.

The site dontkillmyapp.com has per-manufacturer instructions, it's a well-known reference precisely because OEMs break push notifications differently. Worth following the steps for your exact phone brand.
Setting the messaging and mail apps to Unrestricted battery and removing them from the sleeping-apps list made notifications instant again. It was MIUI's optimization the whole time.

cozum: This is almost always aggressive battery optimization killing the app's background connection. Manufacturer skins (Xiaomi/MIUI, Samsung, OnePlus, Huawei) are the worst offenders. Go to Settings > Battery > and set the affected apps to 'Unrestricted' / exclude them from optimization. That single change fixes most delayed-notification cases.
reference_summary: Notifications arrive late or only when I open the app. Resolution: This is almost always aggressive battery optimization killing the app's background connection.

baslik: Computer doesn't detect my phone when connected by USB
soru: I plug my Android phone into my Windows PC and nothing happens, the phone charges but doesn't show up as a drive so I can't transfer files. The cable is fine (it charges). I want to copy photos off. What am I missing?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Charging-only by default is intentional now. When you connect, pull down the notification shade on the phone, there's a 'Charging this device via USB' notification, tap it and change USB mode to 'File Transfer' (MTP). The phone won't appear on the PC until you select that mode.

If the mode switch doesn't help, it's often the cable, many cables are charge-only with no data wires. You said it charges, but that doesn't prove data lines exist. Try a different known-good data cable; this is the single most common fix.

On Windows, a missing/old MTP driver can hide the device. Open Device Manager, look for the phone (possibly with a warning icon), and update driver, or install your manufacturer's USB drivers (Samsung, etc.).
Try a different USB port, preferably a rear port directly on the motherboard rather than a front-panel or hub port, which sometimes provide power but flaky data.
It was the USB mode for me, switching from 'No data transfer' to 'File transfer' in the notification made the phone appear in Explorer immediately.

cozum: Charging-only by default is intentional now. When you connect, pull down the notification shade on the phone, there's a 'Charging this device via USB' notification, tap it and change USB mode to 'File Transfer' (MTP). The phone won't appear on the PC until you select that mode.
reference_summary: Computer doesn't detect my phone when connected by USB. Resolution: Charging-only by default is intentional now.

baslik: iPhone storage almost full, huge 'System Data' / 'Other' category
soru: My iPhone keeps saying storage is full. In Settings > General > iPhone Storage, there's a massive 'System Data' (used to be called Other) taking up like 15GB that I can't tap into or clear. My actual apps and photos are modest. What is System Data and how do I shrink it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: System Data is mostly caches, logs, Siri voices, and temporary files iOS keeps. It's deliberately not directly clearable, but it does shrink on its own when iOS needs space. The single most effective shrink is offloading caches, and the biggest culprit is usually Safari and streaming/messaging app caches.

Clear Safari cache: Settings > Safari > Clear History and Website Data. Then in Messages, set Settings > Messages > Keep Messages to 30 days or 1 year, this auto-deletes old attachments which can be many GB hiding in System Data.

Offload heavy apps: Settings > General > iPhone Storage > tap an app > Offload App. This removes the app binary but keeps its data; reinstalling later restores everything. Streaming apps (Netflix, Spotify) store offline content that inflates System Data, delete downloads inside those apps.

The nuclear-but-effective option: back up to iCloud or your computer, then restore. A clean restore rebuilds the filesystem and System Data typically drops from 15GB to a couple of GB. Tedious but it's the guaranteed fix.
Clearing Safari data and capping Messages to 1 year took my System Data from 14GB to about 4GB without losing anything I cared about.

cozum: System Data is mostly caches, logs, Siri voices, and temporary files iOS keeps. It's deliberately not directly clearable, but it does shrink on its own when iOS needs space. The single most effective shrink is offloading caches, and the biggest culprit is usually Safari and streaming/messaging app caches.
reference_summary: iPhone storage almost full, huge 'System Data' / 'Other' category. Resolution: System Data is mostly caches, logs, Siri voices, and temporary files iOS keeps.

baslik: iPhone won't charge or charges very slowly with the cable that used to work
soru: My iPhone suddenly stopped charging reliably. Sometimes it charges, sometimes the cable does nothing, sometimes it says 'accessory may not be supported'. It's the same Apple cable and adapter I've used for a year. Battery health is still 89%. Is the port dead or is it something I can fix?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Before assuming hardware failure, clean the Lightning/USB-C port, this is the number one cause of exactly these intermittent symptoms. Pocket lint compacts at the bottom of the port and stops the connector seating fully. Power off, and gently scrape it out with a wooden/plastic toothpick (never metal). People are amazed how much lint comes out.

The 'accessory may not be supported' message points at a dirty or slightly damaged connector, or a non-MFi cable. After cleaning, try a different certified cable and a different wall adapter to isolate which part is flaky.

Do a force restart while you're at it (volume up, volume down, hold side button till the logo). A stuck charging-management state occasionally causes 'plugged in but not charging' and a force restart clears it.
If after cleaning it still only works at certain angles, the port itself may have a bent pin or be worn. That's an Apple Store / repair job, but try cleaning first, it fixes the majority of these.
It was lint. A toothpick pulled out a surprising plug of compacted fluff and it's charged perfectly and fast ever since. No need for a repair.

baslik: iMessage stuck on a green bubble / 'Not Delivered' to one contact
soru: Messages to one specific contact suddenly send as green SMS or say 'Not Delivered', while everyone else is fine and blue. This person has an iPhone too. We were iMessaging fine last week. What breaks iMessage for just one contact and how do I fix it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Since it's only one contact and they have an iPhone, the most likely cause is on their end, their iMessage may be off, their phone is offline, or they changed/deactivated the number. But there are things to try on your side first.

Delete the entire conversation thread and start a fresh one. A corrupted thread can get wedged into SMS mode. Also try sending to their email Apple ID instead of their phone number, if that goes blue, the number's iMessage registration is the issue on their side.
Toggle iMessage off and on: Settings > Messages > iMessage off, reboot, back on. This re-registers your device with Apple's iMessage servers and clears a stuck send state.
Check you didn't accidentally block them, and that 'Send as SMS' is on as a fallback (Settings > Messages) so messages still get through even when iMessage can't connect.
In our case the other person had toggled iMessage off after a repair. Once they re-enabled it, the bubbles went blue again. Sending to their email confirmed the number was the problem.

baslik: iPhone gets hot and shows a temperature warning
soru: My iPhone gets noticeably hot, especially when using the camera or navigation, and sometimes shows 'iPhone needs to cool down before you can use it'. It also drains battery fast when this happens. Is this dangerous and how do I stop it overheating?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: Occasional warmth during heavy tasks (4K video, GPS navigation, gaming, charging in sun) is normal. The cool-down screen is iOS protecting the battery, not a fault. But persistent overheating during light use points at a misbehaving app or a background process running wild.

Check Settings > Battery for an app with huge background usage. A stuck app pegging the CPU heats the phone and drains it, exactly your combo. Force-close it (or offload/reinstall). Updating all apps fixes many of these, as does updating iOS.

Remove thick cases while charging or navigating, and never charge under a pillow or in direct sun, trapped heat triggers the warning. If it overheats specifically while charging, try a lower-wattage charger and a different cable.

If it started after an update, the background re-indexing can heat the phone for a day or two, then it settles. If it persists for over a week of light use, back up and do a clean restore to rule out a corrupted process.
A rogue app (a fitness tracker holding GPS open in the background) was cooking my phone. Force-quitting and reinstalling it stopped the heat and the battery drain together.

cozum: Occasional warmth during heavy tasks (4K video, GPS navigation, gaming, charging in sun) is normal. The cool-down screen is iOS protecting the battery, not a fault. But persistent overheating during light use points at a misbehaving app or a background process running wild.

baslik: iPhone stuck on the Apple logo after an update, won't boot
soru: My iPhone was updating overnight and now it's stuck on the Apple logo, the progress bar froze or there's no bar at all. It's been over an hour. I can't get to the home screen. I'm worried I'll lose everything. What can I do without wiping my data?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: First, don't panic and don't wipe yet. The standard first step is a force restart, which doesn't erase anything: press and release Volume Up, press and release Volume Down, then press and HOLD the side button until the Apple logo reappears and the phone boots. This alone fixes most stuck-logo cases.

If the force restart just loops back to the logo, connect it to a computer (Finder on Mac, Apple Devices/iTunes on Windows) and put it in Recovery Mode (same button sequence but keep holding until you see the recovery/computer-cable screen). Then choose 'Update', NOT 'Restore'. Update reinstalls iOS and keeps your data; Restore erases it.

Make sure the cable and port are solid and let it sit plugged in for a while, a stalled update can resume once iOS re-downloads. The 'Update' option in Recovery Mode is specifically designed to repair a failed update without data loss.

Only if 'Update' fails repeatedly does 'Restore' (which wipes) become necessary, and even then a recent iCloud/computer backup gets your data back. So check whether you have a backup before going that far.
The Recovery Mode 'Update' option saved me, it reinstalled iOS over the failed update and everything was intact when it rebooted.

cozum: First, don't panic and don't wipe yet. The standard first step is a force restart, which doesn't erase anything: press and release Volume Up, press and release Volume Down, then press and HOLD the side button until the Apple logo reappears and the phone boots. This alone fixes most stuck-logo cases.
reference_summary: iPhone stuck on the Apple logo after an update, won't boot. Resolution: First, don't panic and don't wipe yet.

baslik: Can't make calls but data works / poor signal indoors
soru: Inside my apartment I have almost no cellular signal, calls drop or won't connect, but WiFi works fine. My carrier supports WiFi Calling. How do I get calls to work over WiFi, and why isn't it doing that automatically?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: WiFi Calling usually has to be turned on manually the first time, it's not always on by default. Go to Settings > Phone > WiFi Calling and toggle 'WiFi Calling on This iPhone' on. You may have to confirm your address for emergency services, that's a one-time carrier requirement.

After enabling it, you should see 'WiFi' next to your carrier name in the status bar when on WiFi. Calls and texts then route over your internet connection instead of the weak cellular signal, which solves the no-signal-indoors problem entirely.

If the toggle is greyed out or missing, your carrier or plan may not have it provisioned, contact them to enable WiFi Calling on the account. Also make sure your iOS is up to date, older versions hid the setting for some carriers.
Toggle Airplane mode on and off after enabling, and reboot once, so the phone re-registers with WiFi Calling active.
Enabling WiFi Calling in Settings > Phone fixed it, calls now go over my home WiFi and don't drop despite the dead cellular zone in my flat.

cozum: WiFi Calling usually has to be turned on manually the first time, it's not always on by default. Go to Settings > Phone > WiFi Calling and toggle 'WiFi Calling on This iPhone' on. You may have to confirm your address for emergency services, that's a one-time carrier requirement.
reference_summary: Can't make calls but data works / poor signal indoors. Resolution: WiFi Calling usually has to be turned on manually the first time, it's not always on by default.

baslik: S3 AccessDenied even though my IAM user has S3FullAccess
soru: I'm getting AccessDenied when my application tries to read an object from an S3 bucket, even though the IAM user attached policy is AmazonS3FullAccess. The bucket is in my own account. I can see the object in the console. Why is a full-access user denied and how do I debug S3 permissions?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: S3 access is the intersection of several policies, and a deny anywhere wins. Even with S3FullAccess on the IAM user, the request can be blocked by: a bucket policy that explicitly denies, an Object Ownership / ACL setting, S3 Block Public Access, or a VPC endpoint policy. Full access on the identity doesn't override an explicit deny elsewhere.

Check the bucket policy first (S3 console > bucket > Permissions). A common pattern is a policy that only allows a specific role/principal and implicitly denies everyone else, or an explicit Deny with a condition (e.g. requires TLS or a specific VPC). Your user fails the condition.

If the object was uploaded by a different account/role, Object Ownership + ACLs can make it owned by another principal so you can't read it despite bucket access. Setting Bucket owner enforced (disabling ACLs) fixes that class of problem.

Use the IAM Policy Simulator or check CloudTrail for the exact denied call, CloudTrail logs the reason. Also confirm KMS: if the object is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, you also need kms:Decrypt on that key, lacking it shows as AccessDenied on S3.
Mine was exactly the KMS case, the bucket used a CMK and my user had S3FullAccess but no KMS permission. Adding kms:Decrypt on the key resolved the AccessDenied.

cozum: S3 access is the intersection of several policies, and a deny anywhere wins. Even with S3FullAccess on the IAM user, the request can be blocked by: a bucket policy that explicitly denies, an Object Ownership / ACL setting, S3 Block Public Access, or a VPC endpoint policy. Full access on the identity doesn't override an explicit deny elsewhere.

baslik: Can't SSH into my EC2 instance, connection times out
soru: I launched an EC2 instance and SSH just times out, no 'permission denied', it simply hangs and eventually times out. I have the .pem key. The instance shows as running. What are the usual reasons SSH times out (rather than refused) and how do I fix it?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: A timeout (vs 'connection refused' or 'permission denied') almost always means the packets aren't reaching the instance at all, i.e. a network/firewall issue, not a key issue. The top cause is the Security Group not allowing inbound port 22 from your IP. Check the SG has an inbound rule: SSH, TCP 22, source your IP (or 0.0.0.0/0 to test).

Second: the instance must be in a public subnet with a route to an Internet Gateway and have a public IP. If it's in a private subnet or has no public IP, you can't reach it directly, you'd need a bastion/SSM. Confirm it has a public IPv4 and the subnet's route table points 0.0.0.0/0 at an IGW.

Check the Network ACL on the subnet too, NACLs are stateless, so you need an inbound allow for 22 AND an outbound allow for the ephemeral port range (1024-65535). A missing outbound NACL rule causes a silent timeout.

If all that's correct, the instance's OS firewall (ufw/iptables) or a failed boot could be the cause. Check the instance's System Log in the console, and consider using Session Manager (SSM) which doesn't need SSH or open ports at all.
It was my Security Group, the inbound SSH rule was scoped to an old office IP. Updating the source to my current IP let me straight in. AWS even has a 'My IP' button for this.

baslik: Lambda function times out when calling RDS / another service
soru: My Lambda works when it just does computation, but as soon as it tries to connect to my RDS database (or an external API) it hangs and hits the timeout. The DB security group allows the traffic. The same code works on my laptop. What's special about Lambda networking here?

cevaplar.cevap_metni: The classic gotcha: a Lambda placed in a VPC (which it must be to reach a private RDS) has NO internet access by default, and also can't reach public AWS service endpoints, unless you add a NAT Gateway or VPC endpoints. So a VPC Lambda calling an external API just hangs until timeout.

For reaching RDS specifically: the Lambda must be in the same VPC, in subnets that can route to the DB, and the RDS security group must allow inbound from the Lambda's security group (reference the SG, not an IP). If you put Lambda in a VPC but in a subnet without a route to the DB subnet, it times out.

If the same Lambda also needs the internet (external API, S3 over public endpoint), add a NAT Gateway in a public subnet and route the Lambda's private subnets through it, OR add VPC endpoints for the AWS services you call (S3, Secrets Manager, etc.). Without one of these, outbound hangs.
Raise the timeout while debugging (default is 3s, far too short for a cold DB connection) and check CloudWatch logs, a timeout right at the connect step confirms it's networking, not code.
Mine was a VPC Lambda with no NAT, the RDS call worked once I fixed the subnet routing, but the external API call needed a NAT Gateway added. Both then worked.
